blocks.x: I had that from somewhere. What about McHale’s?
McHale’s, she knows a lot about McHale’s.
That’s going to be her conversation. McHale’s was a great club. Mike and Pat McHale
I think about that and Bradley in tandem, in a way.
It was a little more – McHale’s was more of an r-and-b club, although Art used to play there and – South African.
Hugh Masekela played there, but that was about the – they had – but it was more like Sissy Houston. Stuff played there a lot. They had a pretty much . . .
It was a friendly environment, though.

It was a great environment for the music. People loved it. It was – and there was Seventh Avenue South, in the 70s, also, that was a great – Mike and Randy Brecker opened it, that club. Everybody played there. That was sort of like the fusion thing started, all that fusion.
Bradley’s seemed to be a place that you went after . . .
Yeah, after hours. It was really – it started around 11 o’clock until 3, 4 in the morning. McHale’s was sort of like that too. He went late. You stayed . . .

Yeah, Polly. Polly went everywhere. She really did. She amazed me. She would go Monday nights to hear the big band at the Vanguard. She really had her – she loved all the guys. She went – we have a huge thing of, what?, drum sticks now, signed drum sticks. She loved the music, and she went everywhere. At that time it was – the 70s – where did you used to come down to? The Five Spot. Didn’t that move to Eighth Street at one point?
Sitting right on the corner, cattycorner from the Dome.
Then it moved – I’m trying to think – it moved someplace down a little further around a little corner there somewhere.
We used to see Art there all the time, with Javon. That was when Javon was a kid, 19 maybe or – Jazz Messengers. New York, New York. There’s no place like it.
